deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page belongs to Gauss's c. 1800 Latin treatise on the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM). There he writes 1/M(1+x,1-x) = 1 + A x^2 + B x^4 + C x^6 + ..., and section 7 proves that the coefficients are A = (1/2)^2, B = (1·3/2·4)^2, and so on. On the previous page he substituted the series into the invariance M(1+x,1-x) = M(1, sqrt(1-x^2)) and compared coefficients. This gave an infinite family of linear equations in 1, A, B, C, .... The left side of the n-th equation is n^2 N - (n-1)^2 L. Here L and N are both 0 if n is odd. If n is even they are the (n/2)-th and (n/2+1)-th terms of the sequence 1, A, B, C, ....

(a) TOP OF PAGE. This finishes the general description of the coefficients from p.12. The coefficient letter K (fraktur) carries a term ± k·2^{k-1}·[(n+(k-3)/2)(n+(k-5)/2)···(n-(k-1)/2)]/(k-1)!. A second part carries ± 2^{k-1}·[(n+(k-5)/2)···(n-(k-3)/2)]·(1/4)(k-1)^3/(k-1)!. Here k is any odd number. This is the 'split into two parts' form of the right-hand sides written out on p.12.

(b) REGROUPING ('sive ita'). Gauss regroups the right-hand sides into the brackets (1-4A), (9A-16B), (25B-36C), (49C-64D), (81D-100E), .... The general bracket is (2j-1)^2 c_{j-1} - (2j)^2 c_j, with c_0 = 1, c_1 = A, and so on. The first five equations are:
- 0 = 1-4A
- 4A-1 = 3(1-4A) - 4(9A-16B)
- 0 = 5(1-4A) - 20(9A-16B) + 16(25B-36C)
- 16B-9A = 7(1-4A) - 56(9A-16B) + 112(25B-36C) - 64(49C-64D)
- 0 = 9(1-4A) - 120(9A-16B) + 432(25B-36C) - 576(49C-64D) + 256(81D-100E)

General n-th equation:
n^2 N - (n-1)^2 L = sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (-4)^j · (2n-1)(n+j-1)(n+j-2)···(n-j)/(2j+1)! · [(2j+1)^2 c_j - (2j+2)^2 c_{j+1}].
In closed form the coefficient is (-4)^j (2n-1)(n+j-1)!/((n-j-1)!(2j+1)!). Gauss remarks that the universality of the law follows from the computation itself.

(c) CONCLUSION BY INDUCTION (made explicit by me). The last bracket in equation n has coefficient (-4)^{n-1}·(2n-1)!/(2n-1)! = (-4)^{n-1}, which is nonzero. The left side is either 0 (n odd) or (2m)^2 c_m - (2m-1)^2 c_{m-1} with m = n/2 < n. In the second case it is minus an earlier bracket, already shown to vanish. So, inductively, every bracket vanishes: 0 = 1-4A, 0 = 9A-16B, 0 = 25B-36C, .... Hence A = 1/4, B = (1/4)(9/16), C = (1/4)(9/16)(25/36), and so on. That is, c_j = prod_{i=1}^{j} ((2i-1)/(2i))^2 = (binomial(2j,j)/4^j)^2. Q.E.D.

(d) SECTION 8: THE DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION. Put y = sum c_j x^{2j}. Then:
- x y' = sum 2j c_j x^{2j}, i.e. (1/2)x^2 + (1/4)(9/4)x^4 + ... (checked term by term).
- x^2 y'' + x y' = sum (2j)^2 c_j x^{2j}, i.e. x^2 + (1/4)·9 x^4 + ....

The recurrence (2j)^2 c_j = (2j-1)^2 c_{j-1} gives sum_{j≥1}(2j)^2 c_j x^{2j} = x^2 sum_m (2m+1)^2 c_m x^{2m}. Since (theta+1)^2 x^{2m} = (2m+1)^2 x^{2m}, with theta = x d/dx, this reads x^2 y'' + 3x y' + y = (1/x^2)(x^2 y'' + x y'). Multiplying by x^2 and dividing by x gives
(x^3-x) y'' + (3x^2-1) y' + x y = 0.
Thus 1/M(1+x,1-x) is a particular solution of this second-order linear ODE: the AGM is 'reduced to integral quantities'.

(e) LAST LINE (partly cut off). 'The complete integral of the same equation is ...'. It begins with a term over M(1+x,1-x) (possibly 2/M(1+x,1-x)); the rest is struck or illegible. From Gauss's known results the intended complete integral is presumably a/M(1+x,1-x) + b/M(1,x), the second solution corresponding to K(k'). This is my inference, not legible on the page.
errors: No mathematical errors found: every displayed coefficient (3,-4; 5,-20,16; 7,-56,112,-64; 9,-120,432,-576,256) agrees with the general formula, and the derivative series in section 8 and the final ODE are correct.

The induction in (c) is asserted as 'perspicuum' rather than spelled out. It is valid because the left side of equation n is either 0 or minus an earlier bracket, and the last bracket has coefficient (-4)^{n-1} ≠ 0.
The general law for the regrouped coefficients is claimed to 'flow from the calculation' ('e calculo sponte demanat') without proof; it is verified here only for n ≤ 5 (and holds in general).
The final line about the complete integral is incomplete or struck; the transcribed '2/M(1+x,1-x)' alone would only be a constant multiple of the particular solution, not a complete integral.

results.what: Coefficients of 1/M(1+x,1-x) = sum ((2j-1)!!/(2j)!!)^2 x^{2j}, proved via coefficient comparison from M(1+x,1-x) = M(1,sqrt(1-x^2)) and induction
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss (diary entry 98, 30 May 1799; manuscripts c.1799–1800, published in Werke III, 1866/1876)

results.what: The AGM reciprocal y = 1/M(1+x,1-x) satisfies (x^3-x)y'' + (3x^2-1)y' + xy = 0
results.modern_name: Legendre/Picard–Fuchs differential equation for the complete elliptic integral K (hypergeometric equation for 2F1(1/2,1/2;1;x^2))
results.usually_credited_to: Euler/Legendre for K; for the AGM, Gauss (Werke III)

results.what: Complete integral as a combination of two AGM reciprocals (line cut off)
results.modern_name: Second solution K(k') of the Legendre equation, i.e. y = a/M(1+x,1-x) + b/M(1,x)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Werke III); Legendre for K, K'

deep.surprise_reason: This is part of Gauss's well-known 1799–1800 AGM treatise, printed in Werke III and discussed extensively (e.g. Cox 1984). The series for 1/M and the ODE are famous and firmly attributed to him; the page adds only the explicit inductive bookkeeping.

checkable.sympy: n,j=symbols('n j',integer=True); [[(-4)**j*(2*N-1)*factorial(N+j-1)/(factorial(N-j-1)*factorial(2*j+1)) for j in range(N)] for N in range(1,6)] == [[1],[3,-4],[5,-20,16],[7,-56,112,-64],[9,-120,432,-576,256]]
checkable.asserts: The regrouped coefficients of equations 1–5 follow the general n-th equation formula

checkable.sympy: x=symbols('x'); y=sum((binomial(2*j,j)/4**j)**2*x**(2*j) for j in range(12)); expand((x**3-x)*diff(y,x,2)+(3*x**2-1)*diff(y,x)+x*y).as_poly(x).coeffs()[-1:]  # all coefficients of degree < 23 vanish
checkable.asserts: y = sum c_j x^(2j) with c_j=(binomial(2j,j)/4^j)^2 satisfies the ODE up to truncation order

checkable.sympy: import mpmath; xv=mpmath.mpf('0.6'); f=lambda t: 1/mpmath.agm(1,t); mpmath.diff(lambda t: (t**3-t)*mpmath.diff(f,t,2)+(3*t**2-1)*mpmath.diff(f,t)+t*f(t), xv, 0)
checkable.asserts: 1/M(1,x) is a second solution of the same ODE (value ≈ 0), supporting the reading of the complete integral
